title: Why it's never too early to start with sales · hancrafted
description: Why sales must start long before revenue is needed, and the first concrete steps to build a sales pipeline: find your zero-cash month, keep a list of potential customers, make first contact, and track your conversion rate and sales cycle.

slides.text: Why it's never too early to start with sales Revenue arrives months after the costs that create it, so by the time you feel you need sales it is already too late: start the pipeline before you need the money.

Watch your cashflow Costs begin before customers Company setup and the founders' living costs arise before a startup has users or income. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, A Student's Guide to Startups: Startup Funding ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com A high burn rate is a clock It puts a startup under constant time pressure, and the stated remedy is to spend little while working fast. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, A Student's Guide to Startups: Startup Funding ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com The default-alive test Ask whether the company reaches profitability on its remaining money at current expenses and growth; worrying too early is cheap, worrying too late is dangerous. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, Default Alive or Default Dead? ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com
Why sales is more than just selling No speaker notes for this Slide.

Sales is more than selling Your starting model is wrong A founder's initial model of users is always inaccurate, even when the founder is one of them, and direct contact with the earliest users gives the best feedback the company will get. 1 Sources (1) Graham, Do Things that Don't Scale ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com Ask about the last time What yields insight is specifics: ask about problems the user already faced, not hypotheticals, and treat talking to customers as part of the CEO's job. 1 The sources are interviews and users, not sales calls; that a sales conversation yields the same facts is an inference. Sources (1) Y Combinator (Migicovsky), Startup School Week 1 Recap: How to Talk to Users ( opens in a new tab ) ycombinator.com A signal must be costly to fake When one side knows more than the other, an action that is cheaper for a strong type than a weak one carries information, because the cost carries it, not the content. 1 Sources (1) Spence, Job Market Signaling ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Investors read the team In a survey of 885 institutional venture capitalists the management team was the most-cited factor (95%), ahead of business model (83%), product (74%) and market (68%). 1 Sources (1) Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan and Strebulaev, How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions? ( opens in a new tab ) nber.org No study measures LOIs or pipelines Carrying signaling theory over to early sales results is an inference, and a non-binding letter of intent is cheap to give, so it separates strong from weak firms poorly; the more binding the commitment, the more trust it plausibly earns. 1 Sources (1) Spence, Job Market Signaling ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Premature scaling burns cash Blank calls premature scaling of sales and marketing the leading cause of cash loss in a startup. 1 Sources (1) Blank, It Must Be A Marketing Problem ( opens in a new tab ) steveblank.com Friends' orders can mislead Early orders from board members or friends are good for morale and cash but may not show what the business model is. 1 Sources (1) Blank, It Must Be A Marketing Problem ( opens in a new tab ) steveblank.com

Stages of sale Cash waits on paperwork With no contract term, interest on a late B2B payment starts only 30 days after the invoice is received, contract terms may run up to 60 days, and an acceptance step can add up to 30 more days before the clock starts. This is an EU directive; other jurisdictions differ. 1 Sources (1) European Parliament and Council, Directive 2011/7/EU on combating late payment in commercial transactions ( opens in a new tab ) eur-lex.europa.eu The lags add up The sources show each delay separately: finding customers, closing, invoicing, payment terms. That they add into one lag, which is why the chain must start early, is an inference. 1 Sources (1) European Parliament and Council, Directive 2011/7/EU on combating late payment in commercial transactions ( opens in a new tab ) eur-lex.europa.eu

Pipeline tools in practice Late deals convert worse In a dataset of 655 thousand opportunities, deals that slip late in the cycle convert worse, and winning deals involved decision makers early; the report's percentage changes are relative, not percentage points. 1 Sources (1) Ebsta and Pavilion, GTM Benchmarks Report ( opens in a new tab ) benchmarks.ebsta.com

How marketing feeds the pipeline Customers do not arrive alone "You can't wait for users to come to you. You have to go out and get them": getting users is a gradual process, and early numbers look too small only to those who underestimate compound growth. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, Do Things that Don't Scale ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com The marketing hand-off has its own rate In one vendor dataset the rate from marketing-qualified to sales-qualified lead was 68 percent, against a 19 percent win rate further down; stage rates are measured on one company's own stage definitions. 1 Sources (1) Ebsta and Pavilion, GTM Benchmarks Report ( opens in a new tab ) benchmarks.ebsta.com

Watch your cashflow, revenue pulled in Predicted revenue is discounted Investors discount revenue that is only predicted, and founders who count on raising more money often find that assumption false, so projected revenue does not cover present costs. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, Default Alive or Default Dead? ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com

Why watching cashflow is mission critical 0:00 – 0:23 Imagine the wall Imagine you are the founder, standing in front of one wall. Sticky notes, one column per month, yellow for the cash you have, red for the costs, green for the revenue. You have watched a board like this, or you are about to, and you know the feeling when you read the last column. 0:23 – 0:42 Cash decides how long you have Here is the claim of this whole Episode: what decides how long your company lives is not how much you earn in the end, but when the money arrives. This one board comes back three times, and each time it answers a bigger question. 0:42 – 0:58 The route We will go through four questions. Why cashflow is mission critical, why sales is more than selling, how to start doing sales, and why a pipeline takes time to build. The first answer is already on the wall.

Watch your cashflow 0:00 – 0:14 Walk the months Read it with me. January, you start with 100 thousand in cash and 50 thousand goes out. February, another 50 thousand goes out, and at the end of February your cash is zero. 0:14 – 0:24 March has no money March arrives and the cost lands on an empty account, with nothing to pay it. The big number sits in April, one month late. 0:24 – 0:32 Antithesis A million euros is coming, and the company is gone. Right on paper, dead on the calendar. 0:32 – 0:44 Hand over the verdict So find your own February: the month your cash hits zero. And if that is the month you run out, when would you have needed to start selling?

Why sales is more than just selling 0:00 – 0:15 Pain first You may think sales is something for later, when the money is needed. If so, you leave most of its value on the table, because the money is the last thing sales gives you. 0:15 – 0:25 The claim My claim is this: selling early pays out before the revenue does. There are three payouts, and each one is a reason to start now.

Sales is more than selling 0:00 – 0:17 Every talk is research Every customer conversation is market research you did not have to pay for. It tells you where to spend your time and which hypothesis to drop. This is my reading of selling as a conversation, not a measured result. 0:17 – 0:31 Know how well you sell The second payout stays inside your company. You learn how well you sell, and whether anyone besides you could repeat it, because a repeatable process is what lets you hire the first salesperson. 0:31 – 0:49 Trust is the sum The third is trust. Investors and reluctant customers trust what someone else has already bought. To be straight about it, that is a claim and not a proof: a first result shows that your team can sell, and that is why it counts. 0:49 – 1:00 Verdict Insight and process both end in trust, so look at the three boxes and ask yourself which one your next investor would ask about first.

How to start doing sales 0:00 – 0:16 Backward chaining Start from the end and walk backwards. The end is a signed contract, and you walk back until the next step is in your own hands, because do sales is too vague to start on a Monday. 0:16 – 0:28 The claim Here is the claim: sales has three stages, leads, opportunities and closing. The first steps are ones you control, and only after them does it become a numbers game. 0:28 – 0:39 Signposting We go left to right. First the stages, then a deal board to track them, then marketing, and then the cashflow board once more.

Stages of sale 0:00 – 0:13 Leads, step one The first step is lead generation. Research and keep a list of potential customers, with names, not a feeling. Start the list this week, and maintain it every week after that. 0:13 – 0:27 First contact, step two The second step is first contact. Cold call, call back an inbound lead, or ask your network, and pick one of them. Make that first call, because that is what opens opportunities. 0:27 – 0:41 Opportunities are the work An opportunity means interest, and interest is not a deal. Follow-up, material, meetings and negotiation are the hard part of sales, and they take calendar time that you cannot compress with willpower. 0:41 – 0:54 Closing is not cash Even a signed contract is not cash. After it come production, delivery and customer success, and only then the invoice, so every stage pushes the money further to the right.

Pipeline tools in practice 0:00 – 0:12 One place for every deal A deal board is the cashflow board for sales. Every prospect is a card, every stage is a column, so the whole pipeline sits in one place. 0:12 – 0:27 Read it at a glance You read it at a glance: what sits in each stage, what it is worth per column, and the next step per deal. On a Monday morning, it tells you where to spend your week. 0:27 – 0:38 Start small So start small. Track your deals in a simple pipeline, and know that a spreadsheet is enough. The tool is not the point, the habit is.

How marketing feeds the pipeline 0:00 – 0:11 Two ways in There are two ways to get a lead. You go and get it, or it walks in on its own, and marketing is the second way. 0:11 – 0:23 Volume into a defined stage Marketing speaks to many people at once, so that a customer enters themselves into a defined stage. An inbound lead is one example, an e-commerce checkout is another. 0:23 – 0:36 Hand to sales Marketing fills the stage and sales works what lands in it. Which means marketing does not replace the first call, it gives that call someone to be made to.

Watch your cashflow, revenue pulled in 0:00 – 0:06 Callback Second time on this board. Same notes, same costs, and one thing has moved. 0:06 – 0:18 Timing, not amount The amount did not change, one month did. The company lives. The same million, a month earlier, and that is the whole difference between a company and a story. 0:18 – 0:32 How it moves Now, how does a note move? A deal lands earlier only if the first call came earlier. So build your own month-by-month board, find your zero-cash month, and count back from it.

Why building an effective sales pipeline takes time 0:00 – 0:10 The obvious objection So the obvious objection: I start selling in January, and the April revenue lands in March? It does not work like a switch. 0:10 – 0:19 The claim A pipeline is built, measured and tuned, and that takes months. Three words describe it: funnel, conversion rate and sales cycle.

Start before you need the money 0:00 – 0:07 Back to the wall Back to the wall, one last time, with the answer to the question we opened with. 0:07 – 0:14 Peak-end close I will close with the four steps, one honest caveat and a small offer. Here they come.
